title: Methodology
introduction: This chapter presents the methodology for evaluating machine learning approaches to network intrusion detection.

sections.title: Dataset Description
sections.content_html:
The NSL-KDD dataset (Tavallaee et al., 2009) addresses limitations of KDD Cup 1999 by eliminating duplicates. Training set: 63,280 records (53.21% normal, 46.79% attack). Test set: 22,544 records (43.08% normal, 56.92% attack). The distributional shift tests model robustness.

Features span four categories: basic connection, content, time-based, and host-based. After one-hot encoding categorical variables, feature space expands to 121 dimensions. The test set includes attack variants absent from training, testing generalization.

tables.caption: NSL-KDD Dataset Statistics
tables.description: The training set contains 63,280 network connection records with a near-balanced class distribution (53.21% normal, 46.79% attack), providing sufficient data for effective learning of both classes. The test set's 22,544 records exhibit a shifted distribution (43.08% normal, 56.92% attack), deliberately testing model robustness to varying attack prevalence encountered in real-world deployments. The 121 features result from one-hot encoding the original 41 features.

figures.caption: Dataset size comparison between training and test sets
figures.description: This bar chart compares the sizes of the training and test partitions in the NSL-KDD dataset. The training set contains 63,280 network connection records while the test set comprises 22,544 records, representing an approximate 74%-26% split. This partition ratio follows standard machine learning practice, providing sufficient training data for model learning while reserving adequate samples for unbiased performance evaluation.

figures.caption: Class distribution across training and test partitions
figures.description: This stacked bar chart illustrates the class distribution differences between training and test sets. The training set exhibits a slight majority of normal traffic (53.21%) compared to attacks (46.79%), while the test set reverses this pattern with attacks comprising 56.92% and normal traffic 43.08%. This intentional distributional shift tests whether models can maintain performance when class balance differs from training conditions.

sections.title: Data Preprocessing
sections.content_html: Preprocessing pipeline: (1) Removed zero-variance feature num_outbound_cmds, (2) One-hot encoded categorical variables (protocol_type, service, flag) into 84 binary columns, (3) Binary label encoding (attack=1, normal=0), (4) MinMaxScaler on numeric features using training statistics only to prevent data leakage.

tables.caption: Feature Preprocessing Summary
tables.description: The three categorical features (protocol_type with 3 categories, service with 70 categories, and flag with 11 categories) were transformed into 84 binary columns using one-hot encoding, preventing models from incorrectly interpreting categorical values as ordinal. The 37 numeric features underwent MinMax scaling to normalize their ranges to [0,1], ensuring features with larger magnitudes do not dominate the learning process. Scaling parameters were computed solely from training data to prevent data leakage.

sections.title: Model Selection and Optimization
sections.content_html:
Each student followed structured selection: baseline establishment with default parameters, grid search with 5-fold stratified CV, and final validation.

Search spaces: BaggingClassifier (40 combinations) → n_estimators=150, max_samples=0.85. DecisionTreeClassifier (36 combinations) → max_depth=20. RidgeClassifier (18 combinations) → alpha=1.0 (default confirmed underfitting).

tables.caption: Final Model Configurations
tables.description: The BaggingClassifier employs 150 decision tree base estimators, each trained on 85% bootstrap samples—providing sufficient ensemble diversity for variance reduction while maintaining individual tree strength. The DecisionTreeClassifier uses maximum depth of 20, identified through grid search as the optimal balance between capturing complex patterns and preventing overfitting. The RidgeClassifier relies on balanced class weights as its primary optimization, as the linear model's fundamental limitation cannot be addressed through hyperparameter tuning.

sections.title: Evaluation Metrics
sections.content_html: Given class imbalance, multiple metrics employed (Chicco & Jurman, 2020): Balanced Accuracy (mean of sensitivity and specificity), MCC (considers all confusion matrix quadrants), Attack Detection Rate (recall for attacks), False Alarm Rate (FP rate on normal traffic), and F1-Score.

sections.title: Cross-Validation and Bias-Variance Analysis
sections.content_html:
5-Fold Stratified CV: Training data partitioned maintaining class proportions; results reported as mean ± SD (Kohavi, 1995).

Bias-Variance Decomposition: Bootstrap-based analysis (200 samples) characterized error sources—bias (systematic error from model assumptions), variance (sensitivity to training data), and expected loss (Geman et al., 1992).

sections.title: Implementation
sections.content_html: Python with scikit-learn, pandas, and mlxtend. Random seed 42 for reproducibility. All models evaluated on identical test set (22,544 records).
